segments.text: Well, Cindy, thank you for joining us
today. We appreciate your time.
>> Of course, it's great to be here.
>> We were just talking about you say
you're feeling a lot of momentum. We're
now just days away from the election.
Let's talk about that momentum that you
perceive.
>> Yeah, you know, there's a lot of people
getting out to vote early, which usually
is a good sign in terms of people being
engaged and that's really what I've been
seeing across the state the past several
months. I've done over 80 town halls
across Kansas. A lot of people getting
engaged who normally haven't been
involved in politics before. Part of
that is because of the tariffs and some
of the policies coming from the federal
level and then the fact that on the
state level, we have an affordability
crisis and nothing has been done by my
opponent who's the Senate President and
his allies who have a super majority.
So,
we're in this time frame where like I
said, there's an affordability crisis,
lack of access to affordable housing,
health care and child care and my
opponent has had a super majority at his
disposal as Senate President and yet
those issues have been solved. So,
people are anxious. People are getting
to the polls. People are looking for
change in someone who will be fighting
for them and I'm that person that's
going to be fighting for them.
>> Well, on this very day that we're doing
this interview, President Trump is in
Wichita
trying to gain support for Roger
Marshall.
Let's discuss what you feel that means
for the current state of politics in
Kansas because it's pretty rare for a
sitting president to
campaign in such a red state as Kansas
but yet here the president is.
>> Yeah, it means they're scared and here's
why. They have spent probably close to
20 million dollars against me in the
governor's race alone. Yet the polls are
tied and you know, this is a red leaning
state. So, what that tells me again,
they're scared because their message
isn't resonating. Time master, so my
opponent doesn't have a record to
deliver to talk about or to stand on in
terms of delivering for the people. He's
delivered for billionaires and
corporations, but hasn't addressed any
of these issues that are facing the
people when he has had the numbers to do
it and could have solved any of those
issues. So, again, lots of bad policies
coming from the federal level, lack of
solving these problems on the state
level by my opponent. So, like I said,
that's what I'm seeing out there in
terms of where we are at this point of
time.
>> Let's talk about the differences between
you you've brought up your opponent
twice now. Let's talk about the
the differences that we're in the
closing days of this
>> Mhm.
>> this campaign.
What are you telling voters that the big
differences between you and Tim
Masterson?
>> Mhm.
Again, I'm here fighting for the people.
I grew up on a farm, the granddaughter
of tenant farmers. I come from a
military family and a union family. You
know, those are my roots. So, I fight
hard for working families and I fight
hard for public education because that's
the key for so many of us to, you know,
to have that upward mobility. My
opponent, on the other hand, has been
hostile to public education, has worked
to defund it and destroy it. That's not
where the people are. People like our
public schools. Additionally, he was an
architect of the Brownback experiment,
the very
experiment, trickle-down economics, that
he, along with Sam Brownback, brought to
the state that nearly destroyed it and
drove us into bankruptcy. He was a main
architect. I, on the other hand, I
established a bipartisan coalition that
ended the experiment to get us back on
track. And here's what we know. When I
helped end that experiment, my opponent,
Tim Masterson, said the experiment
didn't go far enough. That should be a
warning to all of us in terms of where
he would take us and our state. So,
there are clear differences in terms of
where he is. Additionally, I'm a
proponent of legalizing cannabis.
Masterson's always been on the opposite
side of that issue. I'm a proponent of
expanding Medicaid. Tim Masterson has
worked to stop it time and time again.
But, honestly, one of the biggest
differences comes down really to our
values.
You know, over the past several years,
Masterson has benefited from a no-show
job. A job where he's taken in over a
million dollars, didn't have to show up
to it. You know, all the rest of us are
working hard to pay our bills. Some
folks working two and three jobs. And
Masterson has stopped minimum wage
increases. I've brought forward those
bills. Our minimum wage here in Kansas
is 7 and a quarter. And you know what?
To me, that's corrupt in terms of the
fact that we have people out there
making poverty wages, working hard while
Masterson is taking home a million
dollars for a no-show job. Me, I'm going
to fight for the people. I'm going to
fight for better wages for them.
>> Farmers are facing You know, we're all
facing high prices, but it's really
affecting farmers in Kansas. What would
you do if elected to help Kansas farmers
and ranchers?
>> Well, here's the thing. I will push
back.
You know, some of those policies are
coming from the federal level, the
tariffs, the importing of beef. And
you're right, we're seeing high gas
prices and diesel prices. That is
absolutely hurting our farmers and
driving up prices. I'm going to push
back on those things when there are
policies that are bad for Kansas and our
economy and our people. But my opponent,
Ty Masterson, was handpicked by the
Trump administration to be the nominee,
endorsed by him, backed by him. He's not
going to push back. He's going to be a
cheerleader for all this chaos. I'm
going to fight for the people and what's
right for Kansans.
>> ICE was recently in Southwest Kansas
holding raids.
There was pushback
from politicians on both sides of the
aisle.
The Kansas Cattle Association came out
and said that they they wanted to see
more time. They wanted to hear from the
federal authorities before they came
into Kansas. What's your stance on that?
>> Yeah. I went to South Southwest Kansas
the week after that happened and talked
to folks there. And it is people all
across the political spectrum that are
very concerned about what has happened
there and very much opposed. You know, I
will say this, we need immigration
reform. That comes from the federal
level and I will gladly work with
federal officials, our congress people
to make that happen.
Not just the Biden administration, but
the Trump administration have failed us
on delivering sound policy and
immigration reform. But like I said, I'm
happy to work with those partners to
move that forward. What we've seen
happen here recently very much crosses
the line. I mean, we need immigration
reform and we need ICE to, you know,
whoever these officials are to be
pursuing and stopping drugs from coming
into the country and criminals, but not
taking our farm hands or workers. I
mean, these are often law-abiding folks
in our country working hard and paying
taxes. Again, ICE is supposed to go
after the criminals and prevent drugs
from coming into country, not taking our
workers.
>> Uh data centers have become a hot-button
issue
in the last several months. You came out
initially in support. Now you say you're
against. Uh some have accused you of
flip-flopping. What say you?
>> So I'm not totally against them. And
here's the thing, when we got that first
bill about 16 months ago in the
legislature, it was painted as this
picture of bringing jobs
and how it would help the economy and
and how it would help our communities.
What we've seen over the process of time
is we've seen some things out there,
maybe some bad actors,
where we we haven't seen the jobs
manifest. And folks are telling me
through these 80 town halls that they're
worried about their water. They're
worried about their utility rates. And
in some states, we've seen examples of
utility rates going up by 80%.
An affordability crisis, people can't
handle that. They can't handle one more
piece of bad news. So that's what's
driving the fear. Now I know this, we
have data centers out there and they can
be built responsibly. And I issued a
call for a pause to make sure we get the
guardrails in place to safeguard our
communities and safeguard our resources
so they're built responsibly. Now, my
opponent, Ty Masterson,
um one thing that people need to know is
in the primary, big AI tech companies
spent over $800,000
pushing him forward through the primary.
He's not going to be looking for
guardrails and statute. He's talked
about a pledge, but a pledge is just
words. We need statute. We need
guardrails in place. So, you've got me
here fighting for the people and their
resources, or you've got AI Ty who's
going to be looking after the companies
who have bankrolled him.
>> All right, you first mentioned when when
we
started the interview that you
your campaign has momentum. How do you
keep that momentum going as we get
closer and closer to election day?
>> Yeah, I keep showing up for people.
Um just like when the raids happened in
Southwest Kansas, I got there
um to listen to the people. Again, I've
done over 80 town halls. I'll be back
out again in a few days making stops in
critical areas. And again, it's all
about listening to the folks and showing
up for them and letting them know this
election is absolutely the most critical
and that their vote counts because often
in these state-level elections, as well
as the House elections that'll be on the
ballot, sometimes 10 votes makes a
difference between who's elected. So,
everybody's vote counts. And again, this
is the most critical election that we'll
likely be facing in our history in terms
of where it's going to take us. I want
to take us forward and build upon the
progress that Laura Kelly has helped us
with over the past several years. My
opponent those, he wants to take us back
to the brown back days um and bring the
chaos from the federal level to Kansas.
We can't survive that and we can't go
through that.
>> Cindy, we appreciate your time. Thank
you for coming in for on the record
today.
>> Of course, thank you so much.
